newsitem.title: UK: UK budget rewards utility shares, hurts exporters.
newsitem.headline: UK budget rewards utility shares, hurts exporters.

text.p: The first Labour Party budget in 19 years made winners out of shareholders in British utility, financial, brewing and property companies, and losers in manufacturers and other exporters, a day after the finance minister unveiled his "budget for the people."
Chancellor Gordon Brown's budget, announced on Wednesday, set out to boost investment in British industry, yet he failed to deliver the clampdown on consumer spending that some expected.
Markets were quick to draw the conclusion that interest rates would be pushed higher in coming months as the newly-independent Bank of England battles to cool the economy.
UK shares jumped to record peaks and the FTSE 100 finished up 80.3 points at 4,831.7, eclipsing the previous closing high of 4,783.1 set on June 13, to climb four percent so far this week.

"The main winners from our post-budget scenario are the utilities," analysts at Robert Fleming said in a report. "Other stocks that gain are consumer issues that are services rather than goods-related such as Scottish and Newcastle Plc, Greenalls Group Plc and Airtours Plc."
And further gains in sterling will hit exporters, the report warned, adding that "most of the companies that lose out are again exporters."

The surge in sterling was also seen depressing the value of the big industrial companies' overseas earnings, while the abolition of the dividend tax credit could require higher payments into their pension funds.
Shares in Imperial Chemical Industries Plc (ICI) closed down 37p, or more than four percent, at 811.5 pence.
British Steel Plc and industrial conglomerate BTR Plc also felt the sting of sterling's rally, closing down 8.75 pence at 141.5 and at 200.5, down 14, respectively.

Analysts at BZW said nearly half of the FTSE 100 companies' pension funds could become underfunded because of the tax credit abolition, hitting earnings. Industrial companies, with their large workforces and high numbers of pensioners, were seen most vulnerable.
In the winners' circle, National Grid Group Plc jumped more than seven percent to a record 259.38p after the utility avoided being hit by the one-off windfall tax, dealers said.

PowerGen Plc and National Power Plc also registered record highs after escaping the worst possible effects of the tax, which is expected to net the government around 5.2 billion stg over the next two years.
British Telecommunications Plc rose sharply after its estimated share of the windfall tax, about 500 million pounds, was lower than previous speculation, dealers said.
An abolition of the gas levy lifted Centrica Plc nearly seven percent to a record 82p, up 6-1/2p, despite its own liability to the windfall tax of 190 million.

Lloyds TSB Group Plc and other UK banking groups shot higher and remained in favour for their domestic earnings, insulated from the effects of sterling's strength, for their strong financial position and for the prospects of further bids and mergers in the industry.

"Financially they are very strong and they are able to grow earnings and dividends faster than the market, and there is going to be more corporate activity," said a senior dealer at one top U.S. investment bank.
Property and brewing stocks rallied after the budget omitted any tax-rising measures against the property sector and dealers decided other measures were unlikely to curb consumer spending.
